To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the peripheral dose (dose outside the treated area) in radiation therapy is about 10% of the dose in the treatment volume.
the dose at large distances is proportional to the square of the field size and to the square of its distance from the source, and inversely proportional to the depth in water.

the peripheral dose (the dose outside the irradiated field) can be estimated from the field size, the distance from the field center, the depth, the patient thickness, the type of treatment machine, and the type of beam.
In summary, our research is concerned with
dose outside the irradiated area in radiotherapy, which can be of interest in the treatment of children, pregnant women, and other patients who might be sensitive to low doses.
peripheral doses from external beam radiotherapy and brachytherapy.
the dose to organs at a distance from the irradiated volume, the peripheral dose ( PD ).
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
for all types of radiation, the peripheral dose is proportional to the square of the field size, the inverse square of the distance, and the inverse of the patient thickness.
for all practical purposes the peripheral dose in radiotherapy can be estimated with sufficient accuracy by the model presented in this thesis.

for all types of treatment machines, for both x rays and gamma radiation, and for both brachytherapy and external irradiation, the dose outside the irradiated volumes is small and is in the order of a few percent of the dose in the target volume.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
PDs in the region of 0.5 Gy can be expected for patients receiving 60 Gy to the pelvis, and 2 Gy for patients receiving 40 Gy to the abdomen.
the dose to the periphery of the irradiated volume can be estimated to within about 30% for radiotherapy and about 20% for brachytherapy.
the dose outside the irradiated region in radiotherapy can be calculated with a sufficient accuracy for risk evaluation.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the PD can be estimated with an accuracy adequate for risk assessment by using a simple model and published data.
, in general, the dose outside the irradiated area is small and that the dose to the perineum is negligible.
, with the exception of brachytherapy, PDs are low, typically below 1 cGy per cGy delivered to the target.
